p: And then just really quickly, how will you be keeping prices down if they’re name brand? I’m assuming it’s because of the tax breaks and incentives that are going to go back into the lowering the cost. But if you could clarify that question?

Yeah, so the– again, the tenant fit out the grocery store. We’re going to have to pay for that. They’re not going to have to pay for rent or for property tax. So, and we’re going to– because it’s city-controlled, we’re going to ensure that that subsidy, so to speak, for lack of better word, it’s going to go directly into the sort of– the discounted basket.

Okay, great. And her last question was just– and I think the Speaker actually asked a very similar question about whether you’re taking into consideration the mom and pop

stores around the neighborhoods and partnering with them?

Yes. So, we’ve had extensive outreach once a site has been announced and we’ll continue to do so, both– again, it doesn’t stop. Once we open the grocery store, we’ll still have engagement as well as throughout the operations. It’s going to be an ongoing relationship.
Okay, perfect. And with that– actually, Gale, did you want to ask more questions before we–

[interposing] I just want to talk about Life Sciences. I know– I’m really impressed with your program that works with young people who are getting into the business. That’s a great program. I know West Side Strategies runs it. So, my question is, is there a cut to Life Sciences in terms of what you’re doing? How do you see that as a growing industry and bringing hopefully people who are from CUNY or other backgrounds that wouldn’t necessarily get in? How are you looking at that?
Yeah. So, I think you’re referring to the Life Science Internship program–
[interposing] I am.
which is a very [inaudible] it’s like we’re going in our 10th year. So, we’re–
[interposing] I’m aware.

super excited about that. And so we have it this summer. And we continue to have Life Science programs as well– both in terms of capital that we’ve had, but also in these workforce development, including the Life Science Internship. But also we have IDA benefits that we’ve allocated specifically for Life Science companies, and so our IDA team is open for business for Life Science companies to come.
So, was there a cut to the budget for Life Sciences, or is it maintained the same?
There hasn’t been– well, this– we had a Life Science expansion fund that we–
[interposing] Yes.

It was part of our Chief Savings Officer fiscal 26, but we still have

$500,000. That was specific– again, as you know, EDC does not get a lot of city tax levy, so for us to find something was really hard, but we sort of restrategizing about that fund anyway because it had been an investment, and then we did [inaudible] loan, and we only had like three we had given, and only two now, and so we’re trying to rethink that. Again, we have– we still have $500,000, but we thought that would be sort of where we could cut, not cutting, you know, these internship programs. And also, we have SPARC [sic] coming. So, we’re– that’s a huge life science campus, as you know, and so we are going to be putting on a [inaudible] for East 73rd this summer, so I hope you’ll be looking forward to that, and then phase two of SPARC which will have a lot of commercial life science after East 73rd.

Okay. And then just quickly, how do you work with CUNY, with Ken Adams, or anybody else? In other words, we all are saying CUNY should be the bedrock to help get, as the Speaker said, a workforce, etcetera, etcetera. So, how do you work– obviously, SBS works. Other agencies work. But how does EDC work if at all with CUNY?

Yeah, we have a lot of partnerships with CUNY including these Life Sci internships programs because that’s a feeder. There’s a lot of other type programs like that where we access CUNY students. But for example, SPARC, we’re working very, very closely with CUNY, because that’s going to be their campus. So, teammates with them like every single week to make sure that that campus is meeting their needs.
Okay. So, that’s the main program that you work with with CUNY?
Yeah, we have other programs, but that’s the largest one right now.
Alright, thank you.
Okay, great. Sorry, just for the record, we were joined earlier by Council Member Banks and Justin Sanchez. And I’m passing it back to you, Chair Maloney.

Thank you. I want to turn back to the questions about grocery stores that were alluded to earlier by a few of my colleagues and reiterate how important addressing the food insecurity in our city is, especially with SNAP

cuts, and through this budget process have seen so many organizations asking for funding to fill in that gap. I wanted to go back to the site selection, particularly for La Marqueta where it sounds like the two criteria– one is whether or not it’s a public site that you already have access to, and then if it’s a food desert. Are those the two primary criteria for deciding locations?
I– another part of it is that it can be built and online before 2029.
Okay.
So, it’s sort of like development-ready.

So, La Marqueta I believe has multiple full-service supermarkets that are within one mile from the location. I– the USDA definition of a food desert is 500 people living more than one mile away from a supermarket. So, just wanted to speak to if there could have been a higher need area to prioritize as the first market?
Yeah, thank you.
And why are we choosing that location?

Yeah. We had to balance a bunch of things. From the DCP measure of enough grocery stores for a neighborhood, it did rank quite low. So, for the per capita that lives up there, it’s a very dense neighborhood that we– it did qualify.
Okay. And the construction timeline for that site will be 2029?
Yes.

I want to also talk about some of the alternative programs to address the issue of food security. So, there’s Fresh, which provides tax and zoning incentives for private supermarkets, Groceries To Go which gives a 50 percent discount for fresh produce, of course the traditional food pantry, and if we looked at as a city government at these alternative options, and also how far $30 million would go through these other avenues?

Yes. so these are all complementary programs. They do serve different purposes, and you know, I can go through the Fresh program if you want, but– because that’s run by IDA. but the idea of the NYC grocery stores is that it’s

city-controlled, and so that the subsidy they’re providing through the tenant fit-out, no rent and no property tax by the third-party operator is going to go directly– because we control it, we’re sure that it’s going to go directly to the food affordability of the core basket. That’s– and also we want to create these like pleasant, dignified places to shop and good paying jobs for workers there. So, all that combined, it’s one sort of effort to create food affordability and accessibility throughout the city. That sounds like not the only solution. All the other ones that you have mentioned are also– we’re all working together to sort of meet those goals, having different priorities or levers.
And the $30 million for the La Marqueta build-out, that’s just the construction, not the actual operation, is that right?

Correct. But again, the operation is going to be done by the third-party operator. So, we’re giving the sort of subsidy for that ground-up construction to the operator to pass on the subsidy for the core basket.

Most models, if not all models, for public grocery stores in the United States operate at a deficit. So there’s, of course, the capital expenditure to get the grocery store up and running. But then what is the projection of the ongoing cost? Are we expecting these will turn a profit? That the rent and tax abatements will allow it to continue without needing further capital assistance? If you could just speak to the economics once the grocery store is up and running?

Yeah. Again, these are– we’re putting in an RFEI this summer, so these things are going to be worked out, but the goal is for this to be self-sustaining operations with– again, with the subsidies that I spoke about, and we’re going to look at exactly how the subsidies are going to be structured for these core basket goods. it’s – the key thing that we really care about– one of the things that is priority to care about is that there are meaningful savings, and there are– not only meaningful savings for these core baskets, but they’re stable, because as you know, food prices can fluctuate. So we want people to be able to budget. They’re going to know when they go to an NYC grocery

store how much the eggs are, how much the milk is, how much the bread is, and so they can budget each week and manage their finances that way.
And it sounds like the stores will be open to all New Yorkers.
Yes.
So what is to prevent higher income shopper from clearing out all the subsidized groceries?
Everyone is welcome to NYC Groceries.
And will– I suppose is there a proforma about how these grocery stores will remain profitable or revenue neutral, not require additional subsidies?
Again, we’re still working all of those details out, and you know, when we put out the operator RFP this summer, you’ll see some of that information.
Will the RFP include a performance benchmark for these grocery stores?

Yeah. I mean, the key to that is that they need to make– that they’re

requiring them to ensure that the food is affordable for the core basket as well as that they have good paying jobs and it’s a pleasant good experience.
And it will it be requirement that they’re self-sustaining?
We’re going to still work out exactly how the subsidy is going to work, because we have to ensure that these are sort of long-term viable and that the subsidy is meaningful for New Yorkers.

One of the other things I want to look at is just the history of other public grocery stores in the United States. So, there’s– and I guess, have you all looked at those examples? What are we doing differently here to make this pilot more successful?

I don’t know all the models, but I know the team has looked at it. I think one of the key things is that we’re looking at a core basket. We’re not offering everything. Although it’s going to be a regular grocery store, we’re having a third party operate who has experience in running grocery stores to manage all the things that are important to run a grocery store, including

inventory, purchasing, etcetera. So, those are the things that we made sure that we were incorporating so that they were successful.

The examples I saw show that it costs– for 250 grocery stores globally through the Defense Commissionary Agency was $1.4 billion per year in federal appropriations for zero revenue. Another one in St. Paul had zero competition nearby but was still a $400,000 federal subsidy.
Yeah. So, that’s the–
[interposing] I guess I’m getting at, like, the long-term–
[interposing] Yeah, yeah.
operations of this, particularly if we’re putting forward a really large capital investment. We want it to be a sustainable solution that’s going to– yeah, a sustainable solution.
Yeah. Yes. That’s the commissary model, so we did look at that model. We’re not basing our NYC Groceries on a commissary model. Again, everything in that store is discounted.
So, this is a smaller subset of groceries that will be–
[interposing] Core basket.

On the $30 million for the 9,000 square foot buildout, that’s roughly four times the cost of standard New York City retail construction. So, can you speak a bit more about why we expect it to be so expensive?

So, this is a ground-up construction on an empty lot under sort of the railway there, and this is part of an entire reimagination and re-envisioning of La Marqueta which spans eight blocks. So, the team looked it at very closely, and you know, budgeted that amount for city capital.
So this is a more complex site than others.
Correct.
For a pilot, did we look at taking on a less-complex site that would cost less?

We inventoried, you know, so many sites. It’s hard to even explain how many sites we looked at, and again the criteria was– we

had multi-pronged criteria which was all the things we talked about, making sure it didn’t– like, for the city’s measure didn’t have enough food accessibility, that it was dense, that it had transportation, and that it could be brought online by 2029 which a lot of the city sites, the developments, are not going to be available by 2029. So, that was really important because we want to get these up and running.
Did you look at leasing existing grocery stores?

So, we have a private site portal that’s open right now for Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island, and so we encourage private owners to fill out the form to submit their property, and it can be a former grocery store, a grocery– like, you know, we’re open to it. But again, it’s going to– NYC Grocery store is going to have its own look and feel, so we want to make sure it’s uniform across the five stores. So, we will still have some input.
And on the budget, the original plan was 30– or sorry, $70 million for all five boroughs, $30 million going to La Marqueta. How are we going to get to five with that budget allocation?

So, the peninsula for example is a tenant fit-out, so it’s not a ground-up construction, and we anticipate with this private site portal that we will also have sites that are sort of ready to go that are already built out in terms of the base infrastructure.
I think those are all my questions on grocery stores. Back to the Chair.
Can I– can I just ask a follow-up? So, when you say third-party vendors are going to be bidding on the RFIs and the RFPs, which type of groups are you talking about? Like, who would be viable?
Current grocery store operators.
Current grocery store operators, okay. So, like Food Bazaar or whoever it is could also bid on those to operate.
Yes.

Okay. Because I do have a couple of friends that are in that sort of industry, and so they were saying that the buildout compared to what they would pay is more. Obviously,

there’s different reasons for that. But so that’s why they were just wondering, you know, how this is going to sort of compete with some of their stores that are in the communities. I don’t know if they’re necessarily right next to La Marqueta or some of the other ones, but I think that there were some concerts that they had expressed about that in terms of how this would impact the local grocery store companies. So, I just wanted to reiterate that point that I think there is that sort of concern out there especially when you look at the cost. And so, yeah, just wanted to uplift that point that you had brought up, Chair.
Understood.
Yeah. Thank you. Okay. Sorry, before we go into more questions, I think Council Member Chanel Thomas-Henry– you had a few more questions, right?
Yes.
Okay.

Thank you, Chair. New York City ferry: so, the mayor recently announced that this summer the ferry would be increasing weekend trip frequency and opening

additional summer routes and offering reservable seats. Will ticket prices be changing at all during the World Cup or over the summer to account for costs associated with the increased frequency?
No.
Okay. And does the reserve seat option come with additional cost to passengers?
That’s the Rockaway Rocket, but that’s always been more than the regular ferry pass.
Okay.

To specific service. And I would just say, I would add to that that it’s increased service, but also we’re going to be using larger vessels, so we want to make sure that we’re really accommodating the greater excitement for NYC ferries over the summer.
Okay. And is there any funding for increased frequency or new routes? I’m just going to plug Willet’s [sp?] Point, for instance.

So, Willet’s Point, we have committed to studying Willet’s Point as a ferry

stop for our ferry forward vision plan report. So, and we made that commitment to the Borough President as well as some other community members. So, we’ll get back to you on some of the outcome of that.
Will any service be available during this increased frequency since there is a Fan Fest in that vicinity?
There’s nowhere to land or dock, so we can’t offer service we don’t– we don’t already have a landing. We can just increase the services to places where we have landing already.
Got it. Do you have any idea of like costs to actually increase the land– put a landing there?
I think it’s site by site, and so that’s what we’re going to study.
Got it. And World Cup: how were the Fan Fest activities and locations determined?

So, we worked closely with the World Cup Czar and City Hall through the World Cup Czar determined those. I think it was sort of maximum benefit. also, you know, cost was a consideration, be we are also having some activities

on our own sites, and those are the public markets as well as our largest campuses. So, we’ll be having watch parties and fan fests and cultural and community programs.
Housing, so you know housing is a priority across the board. We had a wonderful tour of the brand new Willet’s Point today.
Yes.
And so on 20 acres we’re able to plan out for 2,500 units of affordable housing. The school, the soccer stadium and alike, there are an additional 40 acres on that site.
Yes.
what do you think it would take to get the city to take a closer look at that immediately for future development?

Yeah, thank you for that. We’re really excited about everything that’s going on in Willet’s Point related to the housing, 2,400 units, the soccer stadium, school, the public realm, etcetera. So, phase three has not been budgeted for as you know, or contemplated. There are a bunch–

there’s a lot of private owners on that site, so we would have to figure that out, but we’re happy to open that discussion with you. It’s sort of a long term– as you know, phase one, phase two was [inaudible] decades. So–
[interposing] Day [sic] Street will not take that long, okay?
Yeah, we’re happy– I mean, it’s a phenomenal project, phenomenal development. We’re happy to have more continued conversations for phse three.
And Chair, if I may have one more question? Your public markets, La Marqueta, for example, what is the process for EDC to look of creating additional public markets in other districts?
Yeah. Just so you understand, these markets exist for a very long time and EDC has taken over the management for it. We didn’t create these markets on our own.
Okay.

So, but I think, you know, again, we’re happy to have any conversations if

you’re interested in exploring that option for your district.
Definitely am, but thank you.
Great. And of course, Chair Maloney.
I had one more question on retail markets. EDC has three exiting retail markets that you operate, is that right?
Retail markets or public markets?
Public.
We actually operate six, but three we directly manage.
And those operate at a loss right now, I believe, of $3.6 million in FY25.
Correct.
So, that included no direct subsidy to the food in those markets, and we’re still operating at a loss?
Yes.

So, can you speak to the differences in design between those retail

markets and the public grocery stores and how EDC will minimize the operating subsidies in these new grocery stores.

Yeah, these are very different– although they’re both food-related, these are very different. These are for small businesses, sort of diverse businesses, culturally-relevant businesses for that neighborhood and sort of bringing these foods and these vendors there. It’s– you know, it has a– it’s a kind of community place for people in the neighborhood to go. And so a lot of the projects and tenants that we have in EDC assets are not market rate. We want to support these small businesses. We want to support these communities, and so that’s what the public markets are. NYC Groceries is not about, like, supporting small businesses. It’s about running a grocery store and bringing food availability. It’s a very different model.
Can you speak to the affordability of the products in the existing retail markets, if there’s any subsidy and how those are going to compare to the prices in the New York Grocery stores?

So, how we operate the public markets is that we give discounted rent for the tenants, for the people who have their food markets in the public markets, and that’s how we support the small businesses and what they’re doing. We do not monitor their pricing. We just provided discounted rates, tenant rights for them.
So, it sounds like those are more about food security

Exactly. Well, it’s also about bringing sort of those small business culturally-relevant from the neighborhood. In Lar Marqueta you’ll see a lot of different kinds of stalls there. And so it’s important for the neighborhood and it’s like a nice gathering area.

Thank you. So switching gears, I want to talk about the World Cup since my colleague brought it up and acknowledge a lot of the great work that’s been done since our prior hearing. I was on the– one of the ferries with the wrap for the boroughs and loved that experience and the cultural map and a lot of the efforts to get small businesses included in tourist activities while they’re here. And I did want to circle back on some

of the questions we had about the contract with the host committee. And my understanding from our prior hearings is this is on a reimbursement basis, and EDC can see how those funds are being spent. And at the time, we didn’t have a lot of details, so I’m wondering if you could give us a little bit more of breakdown of how the $20 million is being distributed to– how it’s being spent by the host committee, and then the additional $15 million that had been added in 2027 Preliminary Plan.

Yeah, so the $20 million has already been spent and that was for like a lot of the planning, transportation logistics, the sort of cultural and tentative plan for the– all the activity that’s happening right now. The $15 million is being spent now, and the scope of services there is really for these fan fests and these villages, as well as for marketing, like the Dress the City. Just you’ll see– you know, see so much going on, Dressing the City for the World Cup– and also for these- for some community and cultural programming across the five boroughs.

I also want to commend the administration for making it more

affordable to go to the cup. So the work to reduce the cost of NJ [sic] transit and also including the bus service at a lower cost, and part of that was securing 1,000 tickets at $50. The news outlets say that this did not come at any cost to the taxpayers and was released directly from the host committee. So, I just wanted to get your comment on the record on that.
Yes, that’s right. That is not part of the $15 million that’s coming through

And onto the ferries. We see there’s an additional $38 million across FY29 to 2031 to support reconstruction of the 34th Street ferry landing. Is that considered critical to improving safety for passenger and operators, is that correct?

Yes, the 34th Street landing has always been a popular landing and it’s been very crowded and [inaudible] and sort of safety and accommodation. Also, our recent ferry optimization has increased– the way we’ve optimized the way the boats go from station to station has

increased the need for greater capacity at that site. So, that’s what it will be addressing.
Do you know the scope of the work and the timeline for the reconstruction?
The timeline, not yet. We’ll get back to you.
And will the work be conducted during lowest ridership months to reduce disruption?
